comments.text:
A tiny bit of background about Effective Altruism (and my personal opinion):

EA has origins in moral philosophy, and notably Peter Singer's work. But the movement is splitting along longtermist and non-longtermist lines. Personally, I broadly agree with quite a lot of Singer's work, including that I'm vegan for ethical reasons, I agree with effective altruism, and I'm even sympathetic to his defense of what people have derogatorily called "post-birth abortion". I say this to bring across that Singer's work is very different from "mainstream" ethics, but also - at least to me - convincingly argued for.
The core of effective altruism is the notion that if there is no moral difference between saving a life close to home versus far away, and if it is much cheaper to save a 5-year old from hunger than to save a 5-year old from leukemia, then focusing on hunger can be a more effective form of altruism. This part does seem true for me.
Longtermism extends EA by saying that there is also no moral difference between saving a life in the present versus the future. And that influencing the future is even cheaper than influencing anything today, which would conclude that ensuring a bright future is the most effective altruism. I'm not a longtermist and don't agree with this part at all. I'm not convinced by present-vs-future comparison, but more importantly I think that the uncertainty about our influence on the future dilutes the effectiveness anyway.

The intersection between prominent people in the AI community, and people in the longtermism community is noteworthy. And I kinda agree that NIST employees worrying about the association do make a reasonable amount of sense. Not in the least because a lot of longtermism proponents argue for letting even the kid with leukemia starve, in order to reach "altruistic" AGI/ASI a bit sooner. I want to specifically mention that there are no serious works in the field of moral philosophy that support this approach. Even the hunger-vs-leukemia idea says nothing that reduces the importance of fighting leukemia, it is just a thought-experiment to show that fighting hunger is undervalued in the world today.
By devaluing any and all contemporary (actual) altruism, longtermist altruism is (IMHO) just a convenient moral cover for non-religious technologists to do whatever they already wanted to do. Just like "the will of God" is a convenient moral cover for religious types.

It seems pretty obvious to me. Maybe it's because of my English Lit. background, but it's pretty clear. Assume that the statement by Helen and Tasha says as much as is legally permissible.

The statement emphasizes two critical points. 

The first is adherence to the Mission Statement, and highlights a point of emphasis, and therefore the likely point of contention, around not sacrificing the mission to business interests. 

The recent involvement with Microsoft and OpenAI is a relationship that is worthy of concern. 

It is even more disturbing when that relationship is mentioned with regards to the "benefits [to] all of humanity", i.e. public interests and public safety. Those who recognize the potential risks and dangers of AGI/ASI, handing over the most powerful technology on Earth to a potentially greedy and manipulative corporation that has demonstrated that it is not above spying on users would definitely violate their mission.

The second point that is emphasized is "Accountability".Then, very specifically they mention "deception, manipulation, and resistance to thorough oversight".

Well, that's what the rest of us would call "lying". So the inference is, unfortunately, that Sam was creating a business relationship, which MS have also spoken about, but lied about some or all aspects of this relationship, and attempted to manipulate people to misdirect them or hide key aspects of this relationship.

Or as some would say, a lying liar who lies. I find that extremely unsettling, and I absolutely hate Elon Musk, but I am totally behind his lawsuit against OpenAI, which feels like opposite world. But this landscape is almost dystopian already.
